The Accelerated Capital Allowance for Energy Efficiency Equipment (ACA), introduced in 2008, aims to improve the energy efficiency of Irish companies by encouraging them to purchase energy saving technologies. The ACA is a tax incentive for companies paying corporation tax and aims to encourage investment in energy efficient equipment. The ACA offers an attractive incentive whereby it allows companies to write off 100% of the purchase value of qualifying energy efficient equipment against their profit in the year of purchase. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.

The CHP Deployment programme provided grants for selected renewable and alternative heat sources and was designed to prime the market and to establish a supply chain. The CHP Deployment programme provided grant aid towards the installation of small scale CHP, up to 1 MWe at sites with a suitable heat load. While this PaM expired in 2011, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The ReHeat programme provided grants for selected renewable and alternative heat sources and was designed to prime the market and to establish a supply chain. While this PaM expired in 2011, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The Carbon Tax incorporates a price signal for carbon in the non-ETS sector, specifically fuels used for heating and transport. The tax applies to petrol, diesel, kerosene, marked gas oil (for agricultural use), Liquid Petroleum Gas (LPG), fuel oil, natural gas, coal and commercial peat. This measure reflects an estimate of the reduction in energy consumption resulting from carbon tax using short term price elasticities and energy projections under the With Existing Measures scenario.

The programme aims to increase energy efficiency by providing a range of funded services including advice, mentoring and training to participating Public Sector bodies. Implementation of measures to enable the public sector contribute to its requirements under the national target of increasing energy efficiency nationally by 20% by 2020. A methodology update to calculate energy savings associated with this PaM is being developed by the SEAI so, currently,savings have been frozen at the 2020 value under the With Existing Measures (WEM) scenario.

The Supports for Exemplar Energy Efficiency Projects (SEEEP) programme aimed to achieve significant energy efficiency gains through increasing the capability of the supply chain and stimulating direct employment focusing on energy efficiency projects. The Energy Efficiency Retrofit Fund (EERF) provided for funding towards the implementation of a limited number of qualifying energy efficiency projects. Better Energy Workplaces relates to stimulating energy-saving actions in the business and public sectors. While this PaM expired in 2010, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The measure imposes minimum efficiency standards for new dwellings from 2002 onwards. The 2002 Part L Building Regulations was the first in a series of incrementally improved efficiency standards which is now moving towards low to zero carbon housing. While this PaM expired in 2008, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The 2008 Part L Building Regulations for Dwellings were one of a series of incrementally improved efficiency standards which is now moving towards low to zero carbon housing. While this PaM expired in 2011, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The 2011 Part L Building Regulations for dwellings are one of a series of incrementally improved efficiency standards which is moving towards low to zero carbon housing. The measure imposes minimum efficiency standards for new dwellings. While this PaM expired in 2012, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The measure set a minimum seasonal efficiency of 86% for boilers installed in existing or new dwellings from 2008 and 90% from 2011. The 2008 Part L Building Regulations imposed a minimum boiler efficiency of 86% for all boilers installed in new or existing buildings. This was further improved to a minimum boiler efficiency of 90% in 2011 Building Regulations. While this PaM expired in 2022, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The measure is a phasing out of incandescent lights through the Energy related Products Directive (2009/125/EC) and Commission Regulation (EC) No 244/2009. Commission Regulation (EC) No 244/2009 of 18 March 2009 implements Directive 2005/32/EC (superseded by Directive 2009/125/EC) with regard to eco-design requirements for non-directional household lamps. The regulation provides for the phased introduction of minimum efficiency standards for lamps and effectively phases out incandescent lamps. While this PaM expired in 2016, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The measure targets vulnerable and fuel poor homes and provides funding for the installation of domestic energy efficiency upgrades via regional not-for-profit organisations and private contractors. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.

Stimulating energy-efficiency actions to reduce energy usage by homeowners and the general public. Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland grant-aids householders who want to make their homes more energy-efficient by providing incentives towards the implementation of energy efficiency measures including attic and wall insulation and heating controls with efficient boilers and/or solar thermal. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.

Under the With Existing Measures scenario, a total Electric Vehicle stock of  ~327,000 by 2030,representing 12.2% of the total stock, is assumed. The measure was a fundamental shift in the Vehicle Registration Tax and Annual Motor Tax regime whereby vehicles have been taxed on the basis of their CO2 emission levels since 1st July 2008. While this PaM expired in 2020, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The aim is to increase operational efficiency in aviation through international co-operation in air space control. The Irish and UK National Supervisory Authorities (NSAs) created the UK-Ireland Functional Airspace Block in 2008 to create a seamless and cost efficient operation across joint airspace. This has included efficiency in savings of fuel and CO2 emissions. While this PaM expired in 220, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

The Directive lays down the requirements for the EC type-approval or national type-approval of vehicles as regards emissions from, and the safe functioning of, air conditioning systems fitted to vehicles. It also lays down provisions on retrofitting and refilling of such systems. Ex-ante savings are based on EPA estimates of savings resulting from the impact of the Mobile Air Conditioning Directive by comparing a WEM projection with a counterfactual scenario where the Directive does not exist.
Under the counterfactual scenario, it is assumed that 100% of passenger cars and Goods/Commercial vehicles have AC units with a high GWP (>150). This differs to the With Existing Measures Measures (WEM) scenario where a percentage of passenger cars and Goods/Commercial vehicles have AC units with a low GWP. The difference in emissions between these two scenarios provides an estimated saving as a result of the Directive.

Ex-ante savings are based on EPA estimates of savings resulting from the impact of the Landfill Directive by comparing a WEM projection with a counterfactual scenario where the Directive does not exist.
Under the counterfactual scenario, it is assumed that municipal solid waste remains at 2010 levels across the time series. The fraction of recovered methane assumed is the average of fractions for the period 2005 to 2010. This differs to the With Existing Measures (WEM) scenario where municipal solid waste decreases across the time series. The difference in emissions between these two scenarios provides an estimate saving as a result of the Directive.

The Economic Breeding Index (EBI) for dairy cattle is a breeding tool that focuses on improving the economic and environmental performance of dairy herds. By selecting breeding bulls and cows with favorable genetic traits for milk production efficiency and lower emissions, such as reduced methane output, the EBI contributes to the overall reduction of greenhouse gas emissions associated with dairy farming.

This measure encompasses the deployment of renewables in electricity generation under the With Existing Measures (WEM) scenario. Estimates of ex-ante emissions savings for this measure are underpinned by energy projections for electricity generation under the WEM scenario.

The methodology estimating the effects of this measure on GHG emissions reductions is based on the assumption that the amount of electricity generated from renewables (e.g. wind, Solar PV) under the WEM scenario displaces GHG emissions that would have been produced if natural gas was used to generate an equal amount of electricity. From the 2025 reporting cycle onwards, the methodology accounts for the average efficiency of natural gas power plants.

This PaM will be further refined in future reporting following exploratory analyses in 2026 on PaM categorisation and alignment with the definition of a single PaM on page 200 of the 2025 Reporting Guidelines for Integrated Policies and Measures.

The effect of this measure on GHG emissions reductions represents CO2 emissions from the biogenic portion of bioethanol and biodiesel.

This PaM will be further refined in future reporting following exploratory analyses in 2026 on PaM categorisation and alignment with the definition of a single PaM on page 200 of the 2025 Reporting Guidelines for Integrated Policies and Measures.

This measure encompasses the deployment of renewables for heating under the With Existing Measures (WEM) scenario. Estimates of ex-ante emissions savings for this measure are underpinned by energy projections for renewable heat under the WEM scenario. 

The methodology estimating the effects of this measure on GHG emissions reductions is based on the assumption that the amount of renewable heat consumed (e.g. from ambient heat or biomass) under the WEM scenario displaces GHG emissions that would have been produced if an equal amount of heat from oil was consumed. From the 2025 reporting cycle onwards, the methodology accounts for technology efficiencies of renewable heat sources and displaced fossil fuels and accounts for double counting with other PaMs.

This PaM will be further refined in future reporting following exploratory analyses in 2026 on PaM categorisation and alignment with the definition of a single PaM on page 200 of the 2025 Reporting Guidelines for Integrated Policies and Measures.

The Community Energy Grants programme supports sustainable energy upgrades to existing buildings, services, facilities and processes in the community sector. It promotes projects with an aggregation of upgrades across sectors within a single project and favours projects where deeper retrofit can be demonstrated. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.

The Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme (EEOS) is a Government of Ireland energy efficiency scheme operating since 2014. Under EEOS, the largest energy suppliers and distributors in Ireland are required to achieve annual energy efficiency targets. Large energy suppliers and distributors include companies that sell more than 400GWh of energy per year to final customers. These companies, known as Obligated Parties, are given specific annual targets based on their market share within the energy industry. Obligated Parties can achieve their annual targets by financially supporting homeowners, businesses and communities to carry out energy efficiency upgrades. Note that while support is often provided along side another SEAI grant, this PaM only captures the effects of non-grant supported EEOS scheme to avoid double counting with other PaMs. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year at the same level as in 2024 until 2030.

Deep retrofit is the significant upgrade of a building toward nearly zero energy requirements where the whole home is viewed as a system with respect to its energy performance. While this PaM expired in 2021, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

EXEED Certified (Excellence in Energy Efficiency Design) is an energy efficiency design management process. The process sets out steps for designing in energy efficiency and energy management into design projects, for both new investments and upgrades to existing assets. The EXEED Grant Scheme was launched in 2016 with an incentive of up to €500,000 for industrial and commercial businesses to use the EXEED process to design in energy efficiency and energy management into their new or existing assets. One of the purposes of the EXEED process is to move away from looking at energy efficiency measures in isolation. Instead EXEED’s scope treats an asset as an energy system and converges on a solution that ranks the priority of different energy efficiency investments relative to that system. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.

The Support Scheme for Renewable Heat (SSRH) is a program administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) that provides financial incentives to encourage the use of renewable energy for heating purposes. Financial supports include an installation grant of up to 40% for investment in air source heat pumps, ground source heat pumps and water source heat pumps. Under the With Existing Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.

The programme is intended to create scaleable investment in energy efficiency across key segments of the public sector. This includes the demonstration of best practice retrofit approaches, project procurement and delivery approaches, and testing pilot measures. The overall intent of this programme is to create and stimulate a long term renovation strategy in these key segments, grow capacity, and delivery savings. To date this programme has been focussed on schools, and central government buildings but is growing to other areas such as health, third level education, and water. A methodology update to calculate energy savings associated with this PaM is being developed by the SEAI so, currently,savings have been frozen at the 2020 value under the With Existing Measures (WEM) scenario.

The Warmth & Wellbeing scheme is an initiative led by the Department of Communications, Climate Action and Environment (DCCAE) in conjunction with the Department of Health (DoH), the Health Service Executive (HSE) and Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI). It aims to make homes warmer and healthier to live in by providing extensive, deeper energy efficiency upgrades to those in energy poverty that are living with chronic respiratory conditions. While this PaM expired in 2022, it is expected to continue to have an effect on GHG emissions reductions.

NZEB (Nearly Zero Energy Buildings) has been introduced for all new non domestic buildings, it sees a reduction in the energy performance of approximately 60% compared to the previous regulations. Also required is a Renewable Energy Ratio of 20%, meaning that 20% of the primary energy use must be from renewables onsite or nearby. The effect of this measure is estimated through the estimated difference between average energy consumption expected under the 2018 Regulations and the previous regulations multiplied by the projected number of new buildings.

NZEB (Nearly Zero Energy Buildings) will be introduced to all new domestic buildings, it sees a reduction in the energy performance of approximately 25% compared to the previous 2011 regulations. Also required is a Renewable Energy Ratio of 20%, meaning that 20% of the primary energy use must be from renewables onsite or nearby. The effect of this measure is estimated through the difference between the average energy consumption expected under the 2019 Building Regulations and the previous regulations multiplied by the projected number of new dwellings.

Low-emission slurry spreading (LESS) is an agricultural practice aimed at reducing nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions during the application of slurry. For bovines, a target of 60% of all slurry spread by low emissions slurry spreading by 2022 is assumed. It is also assumed that this target increases to 80% by 2025 and 90% by 2027. For pigs, it is assumed there is 100% use of low emission slurry spreading as per the Nitrates Action Plan.

This measure aims to restrict the use of unprotected/straight urea on both grassland and arable crops to provide savings on ammonia losses to the environment. This measure assumes sales of straight Urea are limited to 20,000 t per annum from 2025 on as per NAPCP.

Ex-ante savings are based on EPA estimates of savings resulting from the impact of the F-Gas Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/573) by comparing a WEM projection with a counterfactual scenario where the Directive does not exist.

The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland's (SEAI) support scheme for energy audits (SSEA) offers SMEs a €2,000 voucher towards the cost of a high-quality energy audit. The energy audit may be carried out on buildings, processes, or systems and it is a three-step process which involves preparation, a site visit and reporting. The audit report that compiles the findings will help a SME to understand how much energy a business uses, the equipment and processes that use the most energy and what actions a business should take to save energy, and their estimated cost and impact. Auditors submit a copy of the SME energy audit to SEAI. The audit includes all recommended upgrades, including estimated energy savings. With this data, SEAI calculates the estimated energy savings per audit. It is recognized that not all recommended upgrades will be installed so an estimated audit implementation rate of 25% is applied based on research from similar international SME audit programmes. Finally, an attribution factor is applied. Under the With Existing (WEM) Measures scenario, it is assumed that new savings continue to accrue each year until 2030.
